content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. Depending on the part of the carcass (breast, thigh, wing, drumstick) and the cooking method (frying, boiling, roasting, grilling) the flavor, texture, and nutritional profile vary. The skin is edible and contains beneficial fats, though many diets limit its amount.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
Breast meat is the leanest cut, while the skin contains about 30 % fat.
Chicken eggs are a separate product but often featured together in culinary traditions.
Various cultures have signature preparations: Japanese teriyaki, Indian tandoori, French sous‑vide, etc.
Chicken can be raised in conventional farms or free‑range systems, influencing flavor and texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken delivers high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Especially in skin‑less breast meat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: High protein content helps maintain a feeling of fullness for longer periods.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: Smoked or marinated chicken often contains added salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Chicken skin is rich in fat; remove it when following a low‑calorie diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be fried, roasted, boiled, steamed, or grilled. Breast meat is common in salads, sandwiches, and quick‑cook dishes, while thighs and drumsticks shine in stews and baked meals. The skin can be left on for a crispy crust or removed before serving to reduce fat content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator at ≤ 4 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen chicken can be stored up to 12 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Crab salad is a ready‑to‑eat dish made from crab meat (or crab‑flavored surimi), mayonnaise, fresh vegetables, spices and sometimes a thickening agent. It has a delicate sea flavor, a light creamy texture and works well as an appetizer or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crab salad is a common filling for sushi rolls, such as the California roll.
Traditional recipes use real crab meat, but mass‑produced versions often contain surimi imitation.
The salad is typically served chilled to highlight the freshness of the seafood.
Common add‑ins include corn, green onion, carrot, and hard‑boiled egg.
Crab salad is frequently included in ready‑made meal kits and party platters.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Crab meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat‑based salads, crab salad usually contains modest amounts of saturated fat.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Crab is rich in zinc, selenium and copper, which are important for immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Low cholesterol content and the presence of omega‑3 fatty acids help promote cardiovascular health.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to crab or its surimi substitute.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared salads often contain added salt, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Certain recipes use sweet sauces, increasing the calorie count.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Because it contains seafood, the salad spoils quickly; keep it refrigerated at +4 °C and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve crab salad chilled as a starter, in sandwiches, sushi rolls, or as a side to rice. Garnish with fresh herbs, lemon juice or capers to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at +4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if it develops an off odor or discoloration.

infant-formula-similac-advance-powder-ma.title: Infant formula, Similac Advance, powder, made with tap water

content.title: About
content.content: Similac Advance is a powdered infant formula designed for babies from 6 months onward. It provides an optimal balance of proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals to support growth and brain development. Preparation is done with boiled or filtered tap water according to the label instructions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Similac Advance is produced by Abbott, a company with over 100 years of experience in infant nutrition.
The formula is enriched with DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for eye and brain development.
It contains the prebiotic FOS to promote a healthy gut microbiome.
Each container lists the calorie and nutrient content per 100 ml of prepared formula.
The powder has a neutral taste, making the transition from breast milk to formula smoother.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: A balanced mix of protein, fat, and carbohydrate supplies the energy and building blocks needed for a child’s growth.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA help develop the visual and nervous systems during the critical early‑life period.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D contribute to the formation of strong bones.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, E and zinc aid in strengthening the immune system.

items.title: Healthy gut flora
items.content: The prebiotic FOS encourages growth of beneficial bacteria, improving digestion.

items.title: Cow‑milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may develop an allergy to cow‑milk protein; discontinue use and consult a pediatrician if symptoms appear.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: A formula that is too concentrated or too dilute can cause dehydration or over‑feeding, so follow the manufacturer’s guidelines precisely.

items.title: Water temperature control
items.content: Water that is too hot can degrade sensitive nutrients; use water no hotter than 40 °C (104 °F).

items.title: Shelf‑life after opening
items.content: Once opened, use the powder within 30 days and keep it in a dry place.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Boil water, let it cool to about 40 °C, measure the recommended amount of powder (usually one scoop per 30 ml), and stir thoroughly until smooth. Use the prepared formula immediately and do not leave it at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the lid tightly closed to prevent moisture ingress.

content.title: About
content.content: Oyster sauce is a thick, dark brown condiment made from oyster extract, sugar, salt, and sometimes additional ingredients such as soy sauce, caramel color, and flavorings. It is widely used in Asian cuisine to give dishes a characteristic sweet‑salty flavor with a subtle marine note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial oyster sauce was produced in the early 1920s in Hong Kong.
The traditional recipe involves simmering oyster meat and reducing the resulting broth.
In China the sauce is called “yóu jiàng” (酱油), though it differs from soy sauce.
There are “dark” and “light” versions: dark is sweeter and thicker, light is milder and less sweet.
Oyster sauce is a key ingredient in dishes like pad thai, wok stir‑fries, marinades, and seafood sauces.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Oyster sauce provides iron, zinc, and selenium, which support immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Although in small amounts, the sauce contains trace protein derived from oyster extract.

items.title: Contains amino acids
items.content: The sauce is high in glutamate, a natural flavor enhancer that can stimulate appetite.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Oyster sauce is salty, so people with hypertension should use it sparingly.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to mollusks may react to oyster sauce.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugar, which may be a concern for diabetics.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add oyster sauce to stir‑fried vegetables, meat, noodles, rice, soups, and marinades. It is typically used in small amounts—1‑2 teaspoons—to enhance flavor without overwhelming the dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oyster sauce in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator after opening. Properly stored, it retains its flavor for up to 6 months. Discard if the smell changes or mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pancakes are a fast‑food staple made from whole‑grain flour, eggs, milk, and a small amount of oil. They have a hearty, slightly nutty texture and a rich aroma characteristic of whole grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain flour retains the bran and germ, making these pancakes more nutritious than those made with white flour.
In many countries they are served with berry sauces, honey, or cottage cheese.
Traditionally they are cooked on a lightly oiled skillet for a quick, golden finish.
Fast‑food restaurants often use whole‑grain pancakes as a base for sandwiches and burgers.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pancakes provide dietary fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver a steadier energy release compared with simple sugars.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains are a good source of B1, B2, and B3 vitamins, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: These pancakes contain magnesium, iron, and zinc, which aid muscle function and immune health.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white‑flour pancakes, whole‑grain versions have a lower glycemic index, helping blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Pancakes made with wheat whole‑grain flour can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Calorie density with added oil
items.content: Using a lot of oil during cooking can increase the calorie content, so fat should be used in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some establishments add salt to the batter; those monitoring sodium intake should check the recipe.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve whole‑grain pancakes hot, rolled with fillings such as cottage cheese, berries, nuts, or use them as a base for sandwiches with chicken, turkey, and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. They can also be frozen in bags for up to 2 months and reheated in a microwave or skillet.
